title: AI Rally Faces Its Toughest Test as Chip Stocks Wobble and Costs Mount
excerpt: A sharp selloff in semiconductor stocks and rising questions about the sustainability of AI capital spending are challenging the trade that has powered markets to record highs.
body:
• The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index fell roughly 9% in a single week in mid-July, its largest weekly decline in over a year, even as it remained up more than 60% for 2026.
  • AI spending by the five largest cloud providers is approaching $750 billion for 2026, but rising capex is absorbing a larger share of operating cash flow and investors are demanding clearer returns.
  • Chinese AI startup Moonshot's unveiling of a 2.8 trillion-parameter open-weight model renewed concerns about the pace of returns from U.S. AI investments.
  • A Bank of America survey found 40% of fund managers believe AI stocks are in a bubble, even as the broader rally continues.

The artificial intelligence trade that has powered global equity markets to record highs in 2026 is running into turbulence. A sharp mid-July selloff in semiconductor stocks — the backbone of the AI investment thesis — exposed the fragility beneath a rally that has lifted some stocks by triple-digit percentages this year.

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index (.SOX) dropped about 9% in a single week, its steepest weekly fall in over a year, according to Reuters. At its low, the index was down nearly 20% from its late June all-time high, flirting with bear market territory — even as it remained up more than 60% for the year.

What Triggered the Pullback

Several catalysts converged. Chinese AI startup Moonshot unveiled Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion-parameter model it called the world's largest open-weight AI system, rekindling investor scrutiny of whether U.S. tech companies are getting adequate returns on their enormous AI investments. Reports that Alphabet's Google was months behind schedule on its flagship Gemini 3.5 Pro model added to the unease.

"The pullback reflects profit-taking and rising scrutiny of AI capex sustainability," said Toni Meadows, head of investment at BRI Wealth Management. "Valuations in semiconductor stocks had priced near-perfect demand, for what has been a cyclical area in the past."

"People got way overextended on these names. There are a lot of people under the impression over the last couple of months that these stocks only go up. And if they borrowed money to buy the positions, then they're getting called out of them."

— Walter Todd, Chief Investment Officer, Greenwood Capital

Leverage and Momentum at Risk

The volatility raised concerns about overextended leverage across the market. Tony Pasquariello, head of hedge fund coverage at Goldman Sachs, noted that leverage has built up in retail margin accounts, leveraged ETF assets, and short-dated options volume. The Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X ETF (SOXL) had slumped 57% from its late-June peak as of mid-July, though it remained up over 200% on the year.

Large hedge funds with heavy AI exposure began reducing their positions in top AI infrastructure stocks in recent weeks, according to bank executives cited by Reuters. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 Momentum Index, which tracks stocks with consistent strong performance, pulled back 10% in July even as the broader market dipped less than 1%.

The Broadening Question

The AI trade is widening beyond GPUs into CPUs, networking, memory, storage, and power delivery, according to Ameriprise Financial analysts. While that expands the opportunity set for investors, it also means returns across the AI ecosystem are less likely to move in lockstep, increasing dispersion and making stock selection more critical.

Capital spending commitments among the largest cloud providers are approaching $750 billion for 2026, but the outlays are absorbing a growing share of operating cash flow. Investors are asking a more pointed question: when will this investment cycle start returning capital rather than just consuming it?

A Global Phenomenon with Risks

The wobble was not confined to the United States. South Korea's KOSPI briefly entered a bear market despite being up nearly 62% for the year. Japan's Nikkei fell into correction territory. Europe's tech sector was among the week's biggest losers after its strongest quarterly gain since 2001.

Yet even after the selloff, AI bellwether Nvidia remains up over 1,300% since the end of 2022, and aggregate S&P 500 earnings growth tracked a stunning 47% in Q2 — nearly double what analysts expected a month earlier. For investors in the diaspora weighing exposure to U.S. tech, the tension between record earnings and stretched valuations defines the current moment.
